screens.title: Generic Methods and Wildcards
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how to make methods generic and how to use wildcards to accept related but different collection types. You will see why a method can declare its own type parameter before the return type, how the compiler infers that type in calls, and when to use upper and lower bounded wildcards. We will anchor these ideas with practical Java examples: a generic printArray method, a printNumbers method that reads from any Number subtype using? extends Number, and an addIntegers method that accepts lists that can receive Integer values via? super Integer. You will also learn the PECS mnemonic — Producer Extends, Consumer Super — which makes the choice between extends and super intentional and easy to remember. Finally, we will look at a common copyList utility that combines both bounds so elements move safely from a source to a destination. By the end of the chapter you will understand the syntax, the compiler behavior, and the typical mistakes to avoid when designing generic APIs that work smoothly with the Java Collections Framework. Ready to begin? Keep an eye out for concrete examples and a hands-on copy challenge coming up.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Overview

Generic Methods and Wildcards

Make methods that adapt to many types while preserving compile-time safety.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Learn method-level generics, type inference, and bounded wildcards with concise examples.
Generic method syntax
T declared before return type: public static <T> void method(T[] arr)
Bounded wildcards
Use ? extends T to read, ? super T to write — remember PECS.
Explore Key Topics
Generic Methods
Declare type parameters for a single method to write reusable utilities.
Upper Bounds
Use ? extends T to safely read values as type T.
Lower Bounds
Use ? super T when you intend to add or consume T instances.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to design and implement generic methods that operate on different types safely, explain how the compiler infers type arguments in method calls, and choose the correct wildcard bounds for collection parameters. You will also apply the PECS principle to decide whether to use upper-bounded or lower-bounded wildcards, and identify common pitfalls such as adding to? extends lists or assuming retrieval types from? super lists. Each objective is paired with a short rationale and a visual mnemonic so you can connect the skill to a real coding decision. For example, when you implement a copy utility you will explicitly use a source bound with extends and a destination bound with super to ensure elements flow correctly. When you spot code that attempts to add to a List<? extends Number>, you will recognize that as a compile-time safety rule, not a runtime limitation. These screens frame the tasks you will practice: building flexible methods, trusting type inference, and using bounded wildcards to preserve both flexibility and type safety.

Learning Objectives

Understand the skills you'll practice and why they matter.
01
Design generic methods
Write methods that declare their own type parameters to avoid overloads and make utilities reusable across types. This reduces duplication and preserves compile-time checks.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Use type inference

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
03
Apply bounded wildcards
Choose ? extends T when you need to read T instances, and ? super T when you will add T instances. This choice enforces safe usage patterns with collections.

Avoid common pitfalls

screens.title: What is a Generic Method?
screens.narratorSegment: A generic method declares its own type parameter so that the method can operate on different types without changing the method body. The key syntactic point is that the type parameter list appears before the return type. For example, a printArray utility becomes expressive and type-safe when declared as public static <T> void printArray(T[] array). That <T> is local to the method and tells the compiler there is a type variable named T to use in parameters and return types. The practical benefit is reducing duplication: you no longer write separate methods for String[], Integer[], and Double[]; the same method handles all with compile-time checks. In concrete terms, if you call printArray with an Integer array, the compiler infers T as Integer. A common misconception is that this makes the method dynamically typed — it does not. Type checks are compiled against the inferred T and erased at runtime, but compile-time safety is preserved. Example code in the lesson shows a loop that prints each element and the same method called for Integer[], String[], and Double[] arrays. Reflect on when to use a method-level type parameter instead of class-level generics: prefer method-level when a single utility needs to be generic but the class itself has no reason to be parameterized. What small helper method in your codebase could benefit from its own type parameter?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A generic method declares type parameters before the return type so it can operate on many types while keeping compile-time safety.

content.html:
Core Concept

Generic method syntax

Declare method-specific type parameters before the return type so the method becomes reusable across element types.
Non-generic problem (concept)
Without generics you'd write overloads for each element type or accept Object[] and lose type checks. Generics let one method keep static types and avoid duplication.
Concrete example
<T> public static void printArray(T[] array) {
  for (T element : array) {
    System.out.print(element + " ");
  }
  System.out.println();
}

// Calls:
// printArray(new Integer[]{1,2,3});
// printArray(new String[]{"Hello","Java"});
Why it matters
Generic methods reduce code duplication, keep compile-time checks, and integrate with Java's type inference so calls are concise.
Common misconception
Generics are not runtime polymorphism. Type parameters are erased at runtime, but compile-time checks prevent many errors earlier in development.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Declare <T> before the return type to make a method generic and reusable for multiple element types without losing compile-time safety.

screens.title: Type Inference for Generic Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Type inference lets the Java compiler determine a method's type parameter from the call site so you almost never need to specify it explicitly. When you invoke a generic printArray method and pass an Integer array, the compiler binds T to Integer. That keeps calls concise and readable while preserving the method's static guarantees. A less common case is when inference cannot decide between multiple possibilities, for example when you pass a null literal or use overloaded methods with different generic shapes — then an explicit type argument like ClassName.<Integer>method(args) can resolve ambiguity. Another misconception is that type inference changes runtime behavior; it only affects compile-time checks and generated bytecode via type erasure. To make this concrete, study the example: calling printArray with Integer[], String[], and Double[] shows T inferred as the element type in each call. If the compiler cannot infer T unambiguously, an explicit parameter list before the method name provides clarity. Always prefer inference for brevity, and add explicit type arguments only when necessary to disambiguate or to force a broader type. What call in your code might require an explicit type argument?

keyIdea.title: Type inference
keyIdea.text: The compiler infers method type arguments from actual parameters at the call site; use explicit syntax only when inference is ambiguous.

content.html:
Definition

Compiler type inference

The compiler binds a method type parameter from the argument types at the call site so you typically omit explicit type arguments.
Integer[] ints = {1,2,3};
String[] strs = {"A","B"};
Double[] dbls = {1.1,2.2};

// Compiler infers T as Integer, String, Double respectively
printArray(ints);
printArray(strs);
printArray(dbls);

// Explicit type argument (rarely needed):
GenericMethodExample.<Integer>printArray(ints);
Concrete example
Type inference keeps calls short. Use explicit type parameters only when the compiler cannot deduce the type or when you want to force a specific parameterization.
Misconception
Inference is not dynamic typing. The chosen type is used for compile-time checks; generic information is erased at runtime, but you still get compile-time guarantees.
Check your understanding
If a method returns a value whose type cannot be inferred, consider supplying an explicit type argument to guide the compiler.

screens.title: Wildcards: The Unknown Type (?)
screens.narratorSegment: A wildcard is a special type argument represented by a question mark that stands for an unknown type. You use? when you want to write APIs that accept collections whose exact element types are unknown but related. An unbounded wildcard, List, means a list of some unknown type; you can read elements as Object but you cannot add anything except null — the compiler prevents writes because it cannot guarantee the list's element type. This restriction often surprises learners who expect List to behave like List ; it does not. An unbounded wildcard is similar to saying "I accept any list, but I will not put typed elements into it." That makes it safe for read-only utilities that operate when element type is irrelevant. Concrete example: a method that prints elements without transforming them can accept List and iterate as Object. A common pitfall is to use raw types like List which bypasses generics and loses safety. Prefer List when the method only needs to read generically and you want to maintain type checks. To move elements between collections, bounded wildcards will be more appropriate — which we will cover next. Consider: when would your utility only need to treat elements as Objects and never write to the list?

keyIdea.title: Wildcard ?
keyIdea.text: List<?> accepts any element type but is read-only for typed additions; treat retrieved values as Object unless cast.

content.html:
Comparison

Unbounded wildcard vs raw and concrete types

List<?> means "some specific but unknown element type." You can read as Object but cannot add typed elements. Raw types (List) lose compile-time checks and should be avoided.
Use case: a logger that prints any list contents—you only need to iterate and treat each item as Object.
Pitfall: trying to add an Integer to List<?> is a compile-time error because the specific element type is unknown.
Concrete example
public static void printAnyList(List<?> list) {
  for (Object o : list) {
    System.out.print(o + " ");
  }
  System.out.println();
}

// Can call with List<Integer>, List<String>, etc.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Use List<?> for read-only utilities that accept any element type; do not use it when you need to add typed elements.

screens.title: Upper Bounded Wildcards (? extends T)
screens.narratorSegment: Upper-bounded wildcards are written as? extends T and express that the collection's element type is T or a subtype of T. Use this when you only need to read values as T. A primary example is a printNumbers method declared as public static void printNumbers(List<? extends Number> list). It can accept List<Integer>, List<Double>, and so on, and you can safely retrieve Number instances from the list. The important compile-time rule is that you cannot add arbitrary Number instances to this list because the actual element type might be a more specific subtype. For instance, adding an Integer to a List<Double> would be incorrect, so the compiler forbids add operations on an upper-bounded list (except null). A common misunderstanding is to expect? extends Number to be writable for Number instances — it is not. The extends bound narrows what you can add because the concrete element type could be a subtype with tighter constraints. Practically, use? extends T for producer roles: when the method consumes values produced by the collection. A quick mental check: if your method only calls get or iterates and never calls add, prefers? extends T for flexibility and safety. Can you find a utility in your code that only reads values and should accept any subtype?

keyIdea.title: Upper bound
keyIdea.text: ? extends T is for reading: you can obtain T values but the compiler prevents adding to keep type safety.

content.html:
Process Flow

Using ? extends T

Use when the list produces values your method will read as T.
public static void printNumbers(List<? extends Number> list) {
  for (Number n : list) {
    System.out.print(n + " ");
  }
  // list.add(new Integer(10)); // Compile-time error
  System.out.println();
}

List<Integer> ints = List.of(1,2,3);
List<Double> dbls = List.of(1.1,2.2);
printNumbers(ints);   // OK
printNumbers(dbls);   // OK
Example insight
Because the exact subtype is unknown, the compiler forbids additions. The list is trusted for read operations where Number is the minimal common type.
Misconception: ? extends Number allows adding Number values. Not true. Adding would break lists parameterized with a stricter subtype.
Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Use ? extends T when the method treats the argument as a producer of T values; avoid add() on such lists.

screens.title: Lower Bounded Wildcards (? super T)
screens.narratorSegment: Lower-bounded wildcards look like? super T and indicate the collection's element type is T or a supertype of T. Use this when you want to add T values into the collection. For example, a method declared as public static void addIntegers(List<? super Integer> list) can accept List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object> and you can safely add Integer values. The trade-off is that when you retrieve elements, the compiler can only guarantee they are Objects, not Integers or Numbers, because the concrete element type might be a supertype. That means assigned retrievals require casts if you need a more specific type. This pattern is the flip side of extends: with? super T the collection consumes values. A common pitfall is assuming you can read specific types back from the list without casting; you cannot safely do so. Use? super when your primary intent is to write values into the collection. For example, if you have a destination list you will fill with Integers, declare it as List<? super Integer> to accept various destination types while preserving the ability to add Integer items. What does this mean for APIs that both read and write? Often neither bound alone suffices and you must design a different strategy or use exact types.

keyIdea.title: Lower bound
keyIdea.text: ? super T allows adding T values safely but retrieval yields Object because the list might be a supertype container.

content.html:
Process Flow

Using ? super T

Use when your method intends to add T instances into the collection; the collection consumes T values.
public static void addIntegers(List<? super Integer> list) {
  list.add(1);
  list.add(2);
  // Integer i = list.get(0); // Compile-time error
  Object o = list.get(0); // OK
}

List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
addIntegers(numbers); // Works
Concrete explanation
Because the list could be a supertype, the most specific type you can assume when retrieving is Object. Adding is safe for T values and subtypes of T.
Misconception: ? super Integer lets you read Integers without a cast. Not guaranteed; retrieved values are typed as Object unless you cast.
Quick check
If you mainly write into a collection, prefer ? super T so callers can pass broader destination types.

screens.title: PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super
screens.narratorSegment: PECS is a mnemonic that helps you choose the correct wildcard bound quickly: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter is a producer of T values that your method will read, use? extends T. If a parameter is a consumer that your method will write T values into, use? super T. The strength of PECS is that it frames the decision in terms of intent — what operation do you perform with the collection? For example, a source list for copying elements produces items, so its type should be List<? extends T>. A destination list consumes items, so its type should be List<? super T>. A concrete example follows: to copy integers from a source to a destination, declare copyList(List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination). The source provides elements of type T or subtype; the destination accepts T or supertype and can accept every element you copy. A frequent mistake is reversing the bounds or using raw types. Always ask: do I pull values out or push values in? PECS turns that question into a clear binding rule. Try saying the rule out loud the first few times you pick wildcards — it helps commit the pattern.

keyIdea.title: PECS
keyIdea.text: Ask whether the parameter produces values you read (use extends) or consumes values you write (use super).

content.html:
Core Concept

PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super

A mental model to pick ? extends or ? super based on whether the parameter supplies or accepts values.
Producer (read)
Use List<? extends T> when you only need to extract T values from the collection.
Example: source for copyList — you iterate and take elements out.
Consumer (write)
Use List<? super T> when you will add T values into the collection.
Example: destination for copyList — you add elements into it.
Key Takeaway

PECS gives a one-sentence decision rule: if the parameter produces T use extends; if it consumes T use super.

screens.title: Pitfalls: Adding to ? extends and Retrieving from ? super
screens.narratorSegment: Several patterns produce surprising compile-time errors when you first learn wildcards. One is attempting to add to a List declared with? extends T. The compiler rejects this because the specific subtype is unknown — adding would risk inserting the wrong subtype. The other surprise is retrieving a specific type from a List declared with? super T; you can only retrieve Object because the list might be typed as a supertype container. Another common mistake is using raw types or unbounded wildcards where bounded wildcards would supply better guarantees. Raw types disable generics checks and lead to warnings and potential ClassCastException at runtime. Also avoid attempting to create new T[] arrays — Java's type erasure prevents reliably creating a generic array; prefer ArrayList when a resizable collection is required. To avoid errors, follow these rules: use? extends for read-only producers,? super for write-only consumers, and prefer precise parameterized types when your method needs both reading and writing. When you must both read and write, design the A P I with concrete types or overloads instead of using incompatible wildcards. Which pitfall have you encountered before, and how did you resolve it?

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls
keyIdea.text: You cannot add to ? extends lists and you retrieve only Object from ? super lists. Avoid raw types and arrays of T due to erasure.

content.html:
Common Pitfall

Why add() fails on ? extends

Because the list could be a subtype-specific list, adding would risk inserting an incompatible subtype. The compiler prevents it.
Example: list.add(new Integer(10)) is a compile-time error when list is List<? extends Number> because the exact element type might be Double.
Common Pitfall

Why reads from ? super are Object

If the collection is declared as ? super T, it could be List<Object> or List<Number>, so the only safe retrieval type is Object without a cast.
If you need to both add and read a specific type, avoid conflicting wildcards; prefer concrete parameterized types or split responsibilities into separate methods.
Key Takeaway

When uncertain, ask whether the method will write or read; the answer tells you which wildcard is safe. For mixed read/write, use concrete types or separate APIs.

screens.title: Implementing copyList with PECS
screens.narratorSegment: This activity shows the classic application of PECS: implementing a copyList method that moves elements from a source list to a destination list. The correct approach declares source as List<? extends T> because it produces T items, and destination as List<? super T> because it consumes T items. The method itself is generic: public static <T> void copyList(List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination). Inside, a simple for-each loop reads each T from the source and adds it to the destination. This pattern maintains type safety while allowing flexible source and destination types — you can copy from a List<Integer> into a List<Number> or List<Object>. A frequent learner question is why not declare both parameters with extends or both with super. If both used extends, you couldn't add to destination. If both used super, you couldn't safely read from source. The bounds reflect the direction of data flow. Use this structure whenever you need to move or copy elements between heterogeneous collections. After reading the example, try to predict what happens if you pass List<String> as source and List<Integer> as destination — the compiler will reject it because the element types are incompatible.

keyIdea.title: copyList pattern
keyIdea.text: Use public static <T> void copyList(List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination) to move elements safely between lists.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

copyList implementation

Apply PECS: source produces, destination consumes.
public static <T> void copyList(List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination) {
  for (T element : source) {
    destination.add(element);
  }
}

// Usage:
List<Number> destination = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> source = List.of(1,2,3);
copyList(source, destination); // destination now contains 1,2,3
Why it works
The source yields T elements; the destination accepts T or any supertype, so each element can be added without violating type rules.
Misconception: swapping bounds will fail. If you declared destination as ? extends T, you could not call add(element) safely.
Key Takeaway

The copyList signature captures data flow: read from extends, write to super, and preserve type safety across different list types.

screens.title: fillList: a Consumer Example
screens.narratorSegment: The fillList pattern demonstrates the consumer role: you want to add an element into a list and accept a broad range of destination types. The signature public static <T> void fillList(List<? super T> list, T element) follows the PECS rule — the list consumes T, so use super. This permits callers to pass in List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object> when T is Integer. Inside the method, adding the element is safe because the destination is guaranteed to be able to hold T or a supertype. The trade-off is that you cannot later retrieve the element as T without a cast, since the list might be typed to a supertype. An immediate misconception is thinking List<? super Integer> is equivalent to List<Object> for retrieval. It is not; reads yield Object. Use this pattern for simple fillers, builders, or injectors where your main action is to add items. When designing APIs, prefer clear parameter intent: if you need to both add and then read typed values back, require a concrete List<T> rather than a wildcard. keyIdea.title: Consumer example
keyIdea.text: Signature: public static <T> void fillList(List<? super T> list, T element) — destination consumes T, allowing broader destination types.

content.html:
Example

fillList signature

When you want to add an element into a caller-provided collection, list should be declared with ? super T.
public static <T> void fillList(List<? super T> list, T element) {
  list.add(element);
}

List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<>();
fillList(nums, 42); // OK: Integer is a T compatible with Number
When not to use
If you need to read back an element as T, prefer List<T> because wildcard retrieval yields Object and requires casts.
Use fillList for builders, initializers, or API entry points that push items into a caller-supplied collection.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how to make methods generic and how to use wildcards to accept related but different collection types. You will see why a method can declare its own type parameter before the return type, how the compiler infers that type in calls, and when to use upper and lower bounded wildcards. We will anchor these ideas with practical Java examples: a generic printArray method, a printNumbers method that reads from any Number subtype using? extends Number, and an addIntegers method that accepts lists that can receive Integer values via? super Integer. You will also learn the PECS mnemonic — Producer Extends, Consumer Super — which makes the choice between extends and super intentional and easy to remember. Finally, we will look at a common copyList utility that combines both bounds so elements move safely from a source to a destination. By the end of the chapter you will understand the syntax, the compiler behavior, and the typical mistakes to avoid when designing generic APIs that work smoothly with the Java Collections Framework. Ready to begin? Keep an eye out for concrete examples and a hands-on copy challenge coming up.

By the end of these screens you will be able to design and implement generic methods that operate on different types safely, explain how the compiler infers type arguments in method calls, and choose the correct wildcard bounds for collection parameters. You will also apply the PECS principle to decide whether to use upper-bounded or lower-bounded wildcards, and identify common pitfalls such as adding to? extends lists or assuming retrieval types from? super lists. Each objective is paired with a short rationale and a visual mnemonic so you can connect the skill to a real coding decision. For example, when you implement a copy utility you will explicitly use a source bound with extends and a destination bound with super to ensure elements flow correctly. When you spot code that attempts to add to a List<? extends Number>, you will recognize that as a compile-time safety rule, not a runtime limitation. These screens frame the tasks you will practice: building flexible methods, trusting type inference, and using bounded wildcards to preserve both flexibility and type safety.

These objectives map to concrete tasks you will practice in the lessons. You will implement a generic printArray method and observe the compiler inferring the type parameter from array arguments. You will write a printNumbers method that uses an upper-bounded wildcard so it can accept lists of Integer, Double, or any Number subtype, and you will see why adding to such a list is not allowed. You will also implement an addIntegers method that uses a lower-bounded wildcard to add Integer values into lists declared as List<Number> or List<Object>. A hands-on copyList exercise will combine both bounds to transfer elements safely from a source to a destination. Each practice task reinforces the PECS principle and highlights a common misconception so you can diagnose errors quickly. Completing these objectives will leave you able to design flexible method APIs and reason successfully about when the compiler allows reads, writes, or both.

A generic method declares its own type parameter so that the method can operate on different types without changing the method body. The key syntactic point is that the type parameter list appears before the return type. For example, a printArray utility becomes expressive and type-safe when declared as public static <T> void printArray(T[] array). That <T> is local to the method and tells the compiler there is a type variable named T to use in parameters and return types. The practical benefit is reducing duplication: you no longer write separate methods for String[], Integer[], and Double[]; the same method handles all with compile-time checks. In concrete terms, if you call printArray with an Integer array, the compiler infers T as Integer. A common misconception is that this makes the method dynamically typed — it does not. Type checks are compiled against the inferred T and erased at runtime, but compile-time safety is preserved. Example code in the lesson shows a loop that prints each element and the same method called for Integer[], String[], and Double[] arrays. Reflect on when to use a method-level type parameter instead of class-level generics: prefer method-level when a single utility needs to be generic but the class itself has no reason to be parameterized. What small helper method in your codebase could benefit from its own type parameter?

Type inference lets the Java compiler determine a method's type parameter from the call site so you almost never need to specify it explicitly. When you invoke a generic printArray method and pass an Integer array, the compiler binds T to Integer. That keeps calls concise and readable while preserving the method's static guarantees. A less common case is when inference cannot decide between multiple possibilities, for example when you pass a null literal or use overloaded methods with different generic shapes — then an explicit type argument like ClassName.<Integer>method(args) can resolve ambiguity. Another misconception is that type inference changes runtime behavior; it only affects compile-time checks and generated bytecode via type erasure. To make this concrete, study the example: calling printArray with Integer[], String[], and Double[] shows T inferred as the element type in each call. If the compiler cannot infer T unambiguously, an explicit parameter list before the method name provides clarity. Always prefer inference for brevity, and add explicit type arguments only when necessary to disambiguate or to force a broader type. What call in your code might require an explicit type argument?

A wildcard is a special type argument represented by a question mark that stands for an unknown type. You use? when you want to write APIs that accept collections whose exact element types are unknown but related. An unbounded wildcard, List, means a list of some unknown type; you can read elements as Object but you cannot add anything except null — the compiler prevents writes because it cannot guarantee the list's element type. This restriction often surprises learners who expect List to behave like List ; it does not. An unbounded wildcard is similar to saying "I accept any list, but I will not put typed elements into it." That makes it safe for read-only utilities that operate when element type is irrelevant. Concrete example: a method that prints elements without transforming them can accept List and iterate as Object. A common pitfall is to use raw types like List which bypasses generics and loses safety. Prefer List when the method only needs to read generically and you want to maintain type checks. To move elements between collections, bounded wildcards will be more appropriate — which we will cover next. Consider: when would your utility only need to treat elements as Objects and never write to the list?

Upper-bounded wildcards are written as? extends T and express that the collection's element type is T or a subtype of T. Use this when you only need to read values as T. A primary example is a printNumbers method declared as public static void printNumbers(List<? extends Number> list). It can accept List<Integer>, List<Double>, and so on, and you can safely retrieve Number instances from the list. The important compile-time rule is that you cannot add arbitrary Number instances to this list because the actual element type might be a more specific subtype. For instance, adding an Integer to a List<Double> would be incorrect, so the compiler forbids add operations on an upper-bounded list (except null). A common misunderstanding is to expect? extends Number to be writable for Number instances — it is not. The extends bound narrows what you can add because the concrete element type could be a subtype with tighter constraints. Practically, use? extends T for producer roles: when the method consumes values produced by the collection. A quick mental check: if your method only calls get or iterates and never calls add, prefers? extends T for flexibility and safety. Can you find a utility in your code that only reads values and should accept any subtype?

Lower-bounded wildcards look like? super T and indicate the collection's element type is T or a supertype of T. Use this when you want to add T values into the collection. For example, a method declared as public static void addIntegers(List<? super Integer> list) can accept List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object> and you can safely add Integer values. The trade-off is that when you retrieve elements, the compiler can only guarantee they are Objects, not Integers or Numbers, because the concrete element type might be a supertype. That means assigned retrievals require casts if you need a more specific type. This pattern is the flip side of extends: with? super T the collection consumes values. A common pitfall is assuming you can read specific types back from the list without casting; you cannot safely do so. Use? super when your primary intent is to write values into the collection. For example, if you have a destination list you will fill with Integers, declare it as List<? super Integer> to accept various destination types while preserving the ability to add Integer items. What does this mean for APIs that both read and write? Often neither bound alone suffices and you must design a different strategy or use exact types.

PECS is a mnemonic that helps you choose the correct wildcard bound quickly: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter is a producer of T values that your method will read, use? extends T. If a parameter is a consumer that your method will write T values into, use? super T. The strength of PECS is that it frames the decision in terms of intent — what operation do you perform with the collection? For example, a source list for copying elements produces items, so its type should be List<? extends T>. A destination list consumes items, so its type should be List<? super T>. A concrete example follows: to copy integers from a source to a destination, declare copyList(List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination). The source provides elements of type T or subtype; the destination accepts T or supertype and can accept every element you copy. A frequent mistake is reversing the bounds or using raw types. Always ask: do I pull values out or push values in? PECS turns that question into a clear binding rule. Try saying the rule out loud the first few times you pick wildcards — it helps commit the pattern.

Several patterns produce surprising compile-time errors when you first learn wildcards. One is attempting to add to a List declared with? extends T. The compiler rejects this because the specific subtype is unknown — adding would risk inserting the wrong subtype. The other surprise is retrieving a specific type from a List declared with? super T; you can only retrieve Object because the list might be typed as a supertype container. Another common mistake is using raw types or unbounded wildcards where bounded wildcards would supply better guarantees. Raw types disable generics checks and lead to warnings and potential ClassCastException at runtime. Also avoid attempting to create new T[] arrays — Java's type erasure prevents reliably creating a generic array; prefer ArrayList when a resizable collection is required. To avoid errors, follow these rules: use? extends for read-only producers,? super for write-only consumers, and prefer precise parameterized types when your method needs both reading and writing. When you must both read and write, design the A P I with concrete types or overloads instead of using incompatible wildcards. Which pitfall have you encountered before, and how did you resolve it?

This activity shows the classic application of PECS: implementing a copyList method that moves elements from a source list to a destination list. The correct approach declares source as List<? extends T> because it produces T items, and destination as List<? super T> because it consumes T items. The method itself is generic: public static <T> void copyList(List<? extends T> source, List<? super T> destination). Inside, a simple for-each loop reads each T from the source and adds it to the destination. This pattern maintains type safety while allowing flexible source and destination types — you can copy from a List<Integer> into a List<Number> or List<Object>. A frequent learner question is why not declare both parameters with extends or both with super. If both used extends, you couldn't add to destination. If both used super, you couldn't safely read from source. The bounds reflect the direction of data flow. Use this structure whenever you need to move or copy elements between heterogeneous collections. After reading the example, try to predict what happens if you pass List<String> as source and List<Integer> as destination — the compiler will reject it because the element types are incompatible.

The fillList pattern demonstrates the consumer role: you want to add an element into a list and accept a broad range of destination types. The signature public static <T> void fillList(List<? super T> list, T element) follows the PECS rule — the list consumes T, so use super. This permits callers to pass in List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object> when T is Integer. Inside the method, adding the element is safe because the destination is guaranteed to be able to hold T or a supertype. The trade-off is that you cannot later retrieve the element as T without a cast, since the list might be typed to a supertype. An immediate misconception is thinking List<? super Integer> is equivalent to List<Object> for retrieval. It is not; reads yield Object. Use this pattern for simple fillers, builders, or injectors where your main action is to add items. When designing APIs, prefer clear parameter intent: if you need to both add and then read typed values back, require a concrete List<T> rather than a wildcard. Let's apply what you've learned with two conceptual questions. First: if you have a method that only reads Number values from a list, which signature accepts List<Integer> and List<Double> while allowing you to treat items as Number? The correct answer is to use an upper-bounded wildcard such as List<? extends Number>. That allows reading Numbers while preventing unsafe additions. A common incorrect answer is to make the method generic with a parameterized type E extends Number; that only helps when the caller binds E appropriately but is not the same as accepting arbitrary List<Integer> without explicit inference. Second: imagine a fillList utility that needs to add an Integer to provided lists like List<Number> or List<Object>. Which signature follows PECS? Use public static <T> void fillList(List<? super T> list, T element). This allows adding T values safely. Many learners pick List<?> or List<T> incorrectly. Remember the guiding question: does the parameter produce or consume? Use that to pick extends or super. Let's summarize the essential ideas to take away. First, a generic method declares type parameters before the return type so a single method can operate on different types while preserving compile-time checks. Second, the compiler usually infers method type parameters from call-site arguments, so calls remain concise. Third, the wildcard? represents an unknown type; List accepts any list but is effectively read-only for typed adds. Fourth, use? extends T for producer roles where you only read T instances, and use? super T for consumer roles where you add T instances. Finally, the PECS mnemonic — Producer Extends, Consumer Super — gives a quick decision rule when writing method signatures. Keep these points in mind when designing generic APIs and when debugging compile-time wildcard errors. First: declare method-level type parameters before the return type with public static <T> returnType method(...). Second: remember that List<? extends Number> lets you read Number values but forbids adding typed elements. Third: List<? super Integer> allows adding Integer values while reads are typed as Object. Keep these three rules as a checklist when you design signatures for utilities and APIs.
